notes.summary: Databases begin with Codd's insight: store data as relations (tuples of typed values) and manipulate it with a small algebra — select, project, join — that is declarative and optimizable. The reading is the Redbook (the course's textbook, free online), whose chapter 2 grounds everything: schemas, keys, constraints, and the data independence that separates logical from physical.
notes.focus: Write three relational algebra queries against a sample schema before touching SQL. The algebra IS SQL's semantics — owning it makes SQL obvious.

notes.summary: SQL as the relational algebra's friendly face: SELECT-FROM-WHERE's logical evaluation order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY), subqueries, and aggregation semantics. You learn the set-vs-bag (duplicate) semantics — the difference between theory and practice that bites real queries.
notes.focus: Take one query with GROUP BY + HAVING and write out each intermediate relation by hand. SQL's evaluation order, once concrete, stops surprising you.

notes.summary: The physical layer: databases are arrays of pages (usually 4-16KB), and every design decision — heap files, page formats, record layouts (slotted pages for variable-length rows) — is I/O minimization. Sequential scans crush random access on both disks and SSDs, which is why layout is destiny for scan-heavy workloads.
notes.focus: Design the byte layout of a slotted page on paper (header, slot array, records growing toward the middle). Every DBMS you will use contains exactly this page.

notes.summary: B+ trees are the database's index workhorse: high fanout keeps trees shallow (3-4 levels index billions of rows), all data lives in leaves, and range scans follow leaf sibling pointers. Insert splits, delete merges, and bulk loading are the mechanics every system (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite) implements.
notes.focus: Compute how many rows a 4-level B+ tree indexes with 100-byte keys and 16KB pages. The number (billions) explains why indexes always fit in shallow trees.

notes.summary: Two building blocks: extendible hashing grows directories gracefully as data doubles, and external merge sort handles data far larger than memory with multi-pass merging. Sorting underlies GROUP BY, ORDER BY, and the sort-merge join — the I/O cost formulas (2N passes etc.) are the course's exam currency.
notes.focus: Compute the I/O cost of externally sorting N pages with B buffers, 2 passes. Then check: does one more buffer meaningfully help? Cost math drives design.

notes.summary: The iterator model (Volcano) and the three join algorithms: simple nested loops (terrible), block nested loops (okay), and hash join (the default everywhere). Grace hash partitioning spills to disk gracefully. Knowing WHEN each wins — data skew, available memory, index presence — is the difference between a DB engineer and a query writer.
notes.focus: Compare hash join vs block nested loop for two relations at specific sizes and buffer counts. The I/O arithmetic picks the winner — always let it.

notes.summary: Declarative SQL becomes a plan: the optimizer enumerates join orders, prunes with equivalences (commutativity, associativity), and costs plans with cardinality estimates. The cost model's dependence on statistics — and its famous inaccuracy — explains why the 'bad plan' problem haunts every production database.
notes.focus: For a 3-way join, enumerate all orders and cost each with simple estimates. Watch a 100x difference emerge from order alone — that's why optimizers exist.

notes.summary: Transactions make concurrent access safe: ACID as the contract, serializability as correctness (some serial order exists), and 2PL as the locking discipline that enforces it. Deadlocks (detection vs prevention), strictness for recoverability, and the isolation levels that trade correctness for concurrency close the picture.
notes.focus: Find a schedule that is serializable but violates 2PL, and one legal under 2PL but not serializable — the second doesn't exist; proving that to yourself is the exercise.

notes.summary: Crash safety: write-ahead logging (WAL) — log before data, always — plus the undo/redo protocol and ARIES' three-pass recovery (analysis, redo, repeat history, undo). The buffer pool's steal/no-force policies determine what recovery must fix. Your 6.1810 file-system log is the same idea at kernel scale.
notes.focus: Given a WAL and a crash point, execute the three passes by hand. Recovery you can simulate on paper is recovery you can trust in production.

notes.summary: Distribution multiplies everything by failure: two-phase commit for atomic commit across sites, and CAP's theorem's honest trade-off (consistency vs availability under partitions) — the reason your cloud databases choose what they choose. Replication, sharding, and quorums complete the vocabulary every backend engineer now needs.
notes.focus: Write the 2PC message flow and mark where a coordinator crash blocks participants. One diagram explains decades of distributed-system design.

lessons.title: Analytics: Column Stores and Big Data

notes.summary: Analytics flipped the storage model: column stores (Vertica, DuckDB, Redshift) read only the columns a query touches, compress aggressively, and vectorize execution. MapReduce/Spark moved compute to data at cluster scale. The row-vs-column decision is the OLTP-vs-OLAP decision — the central architectural split in modern data systems.
notes.focus: For a 20-column table queried on 2 columns, compute the I/O savings of columnar layout. The 10x is why every analytics engine you'll touch is columnar.

notes.summary: Checkpoint through the engine room: storage, B+ trees, hash/external sorting, join algorithms, and basic optimization. The exams test I/O cost arithmetic and algorithm selection under constraints — bring the cost formulas you derived in the focus prompts; they are the exam.
notes.focus: Re-derive every cost formula from a blank page (external sort, hash join, BNL). Derivation beats memorization when exam problems twist the setup.

lessons.title: Final: Streaming, Modern Systems, and Synthesis

notes.summary: The close: stream processing's windowed aggregates, the resurgence of embedded engines (SQLite, DuckDB), and the course synthesis. Your final artifact: a written map from a SQL query text to pages on disk — parser, algebra, optimizer, iterators, buffer pool, and log — every box something you could now reason about from first principles.
notes.focus: Write that query-to-disk map from memory. Full Stack Ocean's own MongoDB sits on these exact ideas — reading its architecture with this map is the final exam.
